summary: IMAP normally searches only the selected mailbox. This experimental extension lets a client search many mailboxes with one command, cutting round trips. It was replaced by RFC 7377.

eli5.summary: Instead of looking through each drawer separately, you ask the whole cabinet at once. It was later replaced by RFC 7377.

questions: how to search multiple mailboxes in imap
subtitle: Search multiple mailboxes with a single command

tldr.problem: IMAP clients can only search one mailbox at a time, requiring multiple SELECT and SEARCH commands to search multiple mailboxes, which wastes round trips and disrupts the currently selected mailbox.
tldr.mechanism: The ESEARCH extension adds a new command that searches multiple mailboxes in a single operation, with source options to specify which mailboxes to search and response fields to identify results.
tldr.outcome: Clients can efficiently search across many mailboxes without round-trip delays or disruption, though this experimental approach was later superseded by RFC 7377.

today: RFC 6237 is an Experimental RFC that was obsoleted by RFC 7377, which provides a similar but refined approach to multimailbox searching.

sections.title: The Problem with Single-Mailbox Searching
sections.content: The IMAP4 protocol lets email clients retrieve messages from mail servers. However, the SEARCH command works on only the currently selected mailbox. When a client wants to search multiple mailboxes, it must send a series of SELECT and SEARCH commands, waiting for each one to complete before moving to the next. This creates three problems: it wastes network round trips, it prevents command pipelining (because the server might run commands in parallel, making responses indistinguishable), and it disrupts the client's selection state, requiring it to remember and restore which mailbox was active.
sections.eli5: IMAP normally lets you look in one drawer at a time. If you want to search ten drawers, you have to ask about each one separately, wait for each answer, and remember where you started.

sections.title: The ESEARCH Solution
sections.content: The MULTISEARCH extension introduces the ESEARCH command (the name came from extensions to the earlier search mechanism in RFC 4731). Unlike the standard SEARCH command, ESEARCH can specify multiple source mailboxes and returns responses with tags and mailbox names that identify which results came from which mailbox. This allows clients to send multiple ESEARCH commands at once and correctly match responses back to their requests, even if the server runs them in parallel.
sections.eli5: ESEARCH lets you ask the server to look in multiple drawers at once. When it answers, it tells you which drawer each result came from, so you do not get confused.

sections.title: Source Options and Mailbox Selection
sections.content: The ESEARCH command uses source options to specify which mailboxes to search. Clients can name mailboxes explicitly, search by personal mailboxes (the user's own folder hierarchy), or use subtree to search a mailbox and all subordinate mailboxes below it, or subtree-one to search only one level of children. If no source option is specified, only the currently selected mailbox is searched. For recursive subtree searches, servers must defend against loops in the folder hierarchy by tracking visited mailboxes or limiting depth.
sections.eli5: You can say "look in these specific drawers," "look in all of my drawers," or "look in this drawer and anything inside it." The server keeps track so it does not look in the same place twice.

sections.title: Response Format and Pipelining
sections.content: Each ESEARCH response includes three correlators that identify its origin: the TAG (echoing the client's tag so it matches the request), the MAILBOX name, and the UIDVALIDITY value (a unique identifier for that mailbox's contents). The response contains UIDs (unique identifiers), not message numbers, because non-selected mailboxes do not have meaningful message number sequences. If a mailbox contains no matching messages, no ESEARCH response is returned for it. Clients can safely pipeline multiple ESEARCH commands because the correlators allow them to match each response to the correct request and mailbox, even if responses are interleaved.
sections.eli5: The answer comes back labeled with a tag, the drawer name, and a validity number, so you know exactly which request and which drawer the results are from. This makes it safe to ask multiple questions at once.

sections.title: Practical Limits and Access Control
sections.content: A single ESEARCH command can potentially trigger searches of thousands of mailboxes, which could overload a server. Implementations are expected to impose reasonable limits on the number of mailboxes searched per command or on per-client resource usage. The command respects IMAP access control: the logged-in user must have read ("r") rights on explicitly named mailboxes and list ("l") rights on mailboxes reached through the personal or subtree specifiers. Mailboxes the user cannot access are silently ignored. If the SEARCHRES extension (which saves search results for later use) is also supported, the SAVE result option is only allowed when searching the currently selected mailbox; combining SAVE with other mailbox searches returns an error.
sections.eli5: Servers set limits on how much work one request can cause, and they make sure you can only search mailboxes you are allowed to see. You cannot use shortcuts to look where you should not look.
